name: Space Station
radiationNote: NASA's estimate for 30 days to a year in low Earth orbit is less than 5 to 150 mGy. NASA keeps an astronaut's whole career under 600 mSv. About 30% of the radiation on the ISS comes from neutrons.

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 007: Mission Duration, pp. 4, 7
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 020: Radiation Protection, p. 4
Canadian Space Agency, Monitoring radiation for astronaut health (2026-02-26)

name: Moon base
delayLabel: about 1.3 seconds (light from Earth to the Moon)
radiationNote: NASA's estimate for a long lunar mission with a surface stay (30 days to a year) is about 100 to 120 mGy, and the surface itself is about 0.5 mSv per day. NASA designs surface systems to stay under 0.9 mSv per day, and keeps careers under 600 mSv.

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 007: Mission Duration, p. 4
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 020: Radiation Protection, pp. 4, 7, 14
NASA Science, Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day (Moon distance and light time)

name: Lunar rover
delayLabel: about 1.3 seconds (light from Earth to the Moon)
radiationNote: Surface exposure is about 0.5 mSv per day. NASA expects 3 to 4 moonwalks a week on long lunar missions, so crews spend many hours outside the shelter.

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 020: Radiation Protection, p. 7
NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 007: Mission Duration, p. 4
NASA Science, Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day (Moon distance and light time)

name: Mars transit
delayLabel: up to about 22 minutes one way, depending on distance (14 minutes used as the example)
radiationNote: NASA's estimates are 175 to 220 mGy for a Mars preparatory mission and 300 to 450 mGy for a 730 to 1,224-day Mars mission. In free space the design limit is 1.3 mSv per day, and unshielded cosmic radiation is about 1.5 mSv per day.

sources.title: NASA OCHMO Technical Brief 007: Mission Duration, p. 4
